lines.text: Three real events happen here, each one worded completely differently from the other two.
Each one also carries the same real, typed field attached to it, underneath its own wording. Summed directly, does that typed field give the real, correct total?
Yes, genuinely.
That field was never text to begin with, so summing it directly just works.
Run it for real: summed directly, that typed field gives exactly the right total.
That holds no matter how different the wording is in each of the three events.
Now try getting the same total a different way: by reading it back out of each event's own rendered sentence instead of the typed field underneath.
Does reading the sentences give the same correct total?
No, genuinely.
One of those three sentences spells its own number out as a word instead of writing it as a digit.
Run it for real: read back out of the sentences, the total comes out genuinely wrong, because one real sentence never wrote its number as a digit at all.
Separately, picture one real, specified header, built once from a real trace id, a real parent id, and a real sampled flag, then handed to a completely different parser to read back.
Does it come back exactly as built? And does a genuinely broken version of that same header get rejected, instead of being guessed at?
Yes to both, genuinely.
A real specification is written so a second, independent implementation can parse what the first one built, exactly, and refuse whatever it can't.
Run it for real: handed to the parser, that header comes back out exactly as it was built, and the genuinely broken version of it is rejected outright, never guessed at.

lines.text: One real, independent specification and one real crate's own documentation each name this exact rule in their own words.
A trace id and a parent id are real, specific values, never free text. And a field attached to a real event or span is real, typed data, never a sentence written for a person.

So here's what this topic's own three real runs are really standing in for: a typed value attached directly to a real event survives being summed, filtered, or asked about later, exactly, no matter how its own event happens to be worded.
The same value, once it's only living inside a sentence written for a person, can quietly go missing the moment that sentence is worded any differently.
And a real, specified format carries its own values across that same gap, surviving being built by one program and read back correctly by a completely different one.
